highlights: Gas sovereignty under pressure from European diversification

frictionVectors.title: European gas leverage
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains substantial bargaining power as a gas supplier, but European efforts to diversify imports and accelerate renewables could weaken long-term leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Sahel exposure
frictionVectors.details: Regional instability and diplomatic competition involving Morocco complicate border security, trade corridors, and Algeria's strategic autonomy.

highlights: Critical minerals draw competing external interest

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and oil-price volatility continue to shape fiscal space, while declining mature fields increase pressure for new offshore investment.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: The corridor is attracting Western and Chinese interest because of its access to Congolese and Zambian minerals, creating opportunities but also governance and ownership risks.

frictionVectors.title: Northern jihadist spillover
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and militant infiltration near Burkina Faso and Niger threaten transport routes, agricultural assets, and state control in northern Benin.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin's economy relies heavily on external trade through the Port of Cotonou and regional corridors, leaving infrastructure revenue and logistics exposed to neighboring political instability.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market exposure
frictionVectors.details: Botswana maintains strong state oversight and negotiating capacity, but dependence on global diamond demand and synthetic stones threatens fiscal and export resilience.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and water constraints
frictionVectors.details: Imported power, grid limitations, and chronic water stress constrain industrial sovereignty and increase reliance on regional infrastructure and external finance.

highlights: Resource nationalism rises amid strategic realignment

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation and tighter oversight of gold production, challenging established foreign operators while informal mining remains difficult to regulate.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel security and external partners
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence threatens mines, roads, and agricultural zones, while the shift away from Western security partnerships toward Russia-linked support raises new dependency and accountability risks.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Governance
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater state control and formalization of nickel, rare-earth, and gold projects, but limited capital and regulatory capacity leave room for opaque external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda Border Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Persistent accusations involving armed groups and cross-border support keep trade and security cooperation fragile, increasing Burundi's dependence on non-Western diplomatic and security partners.

frictionVectors.title: Atlantic Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's ports and exclusive economic zone draw interest from the United States, Europe, and other partners seeking Atlantic surveillance and logistics access. Praia retains leverage but must avoid overdependence on any single security sponsor.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Tourism, ports, energy, and water infrastructure remain reliant on concessional finance and foreign investment, limiting full national control over long-term development priorities.

highlights: Oil and minerals remain externally exposed

frictionVectors.title: Resource-Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Hydrocarbons, timber, and emerging mining projects are shaped by foreign operators and opaque concession structures, while fiscal pressures constrain Cameroon's bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and Far-North Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest and insurgency around the Lake Chad basin disrupt roads, energy infrastructure, and state access to productive regions.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security-Mining Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel retain major influence around regime protection and mining zones, creating a sovereignty trade-off in which security support is associated with privileged access to resources.

frictionVectors.title: Armed-Group Control of Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Rebel and criminal networks continue to contest roads, borderlands, and artisanal mining areas, limiting Bangui's ability to regulate taxation, transport, and mineral exports.

highlights: Oil finances the state but narrows policy space

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Pipeline Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal and political system remains heavily tied to oil revenues and export infrastructure, leaving the government vulnerable to foreign operators, price swings, and transit constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Conflict Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Refugee flows, armed-group movement, and instability along the eastern border strain transport and security capacity while increasing N'Djamena's reliance on external military and humanitarian support.

frictionVectors.title: FRANCE–MAYOTTE DISPUTE
frictionVectors.details: Moroni continues to claim Mayotte, while France maintains administrative, security, and economic control of the island. The dispute limits bilateral trust and complicates maritime cooperation.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, foreign aid, and imported energy, leaving limited room for autonomous resource or infrastructure policy.

frictionVectors.title: EASTERN CONFLICT
frictionVectors.details: M23 advances and alleged Rwandan support continue to undermine Kinshasa's territorial control and threaten mining corridors in North and South Kivu.

frictionVectors.title: CRITICAL MINERALS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Western, and regional actors are competing for copper and cobalt access. Infrastructure and processing deals offer investment but continue to raise concerns over unequal value capture and contract transparency.

frictionVectors.title: HYDROCARBON DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: State finances remain highly exposed to oil production and prices, limiting diversification and leaving strategic assets vulnerable to external operators and market cycles.

frictionVectors.title: DEBT-FOR-INFRASTRUCTURE EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain central to roads, public works, and financing arrangements. These ties expand infrastructure capacity while constraining fiscal flexibility and bargaining autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: COCOA VALUE-CHAIN DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is improving local processing and regulation, but foreign traders and manufacturers still capture much of the value from the country's dominant export.

frictionVectors.title: NORTHERN SECURITY PRESSURE
frictionVectors.details: Militant spillover from the Sahel continues to drive border-security spending and foreign cooperation, creating infrastructure and sovereignty risks in northern districts.

frictionVectors.title: ETHIOPIAN ACCESS DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's ports remain Ethiopia's principal trade outlet, giving Djibouti major leverage while making its economy vulnerable to Ethiopian diversification and regional rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: BASES AND DEBT EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: The presence of Chinese, U.S., French, Japanese, and other military facilities generates revenue and strategic weight but limits policy autonomy. Debt and port obligations further increase sensitivity to external creditors.

frictionVectors.title: Suez and Red Sea insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Attacks and instability around the Red Sea threaten canal revenues and raise security costs. Egypt is expanding naval coordination while preserving control over the waterway and its adjacent logistics infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gulf investment and multilateral lending support Egypt's fiscal position but increase outside influence over strategic assets, privatization, and currency policy.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas dependency
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field output leaves the state dependent on foreign operators, opaque production-sharing arrangements, and volatile hydrocarbon revenue.

frictionVectors.title: LNG and port competition
frictionVectors.details: Equatorial Guinea is seeking new gas partnerships and regional processing deals, but external firms retain substantial leverage over capital, technology, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to shipping lanes attract competing regional and extra-regional security interests. The government uses this geography to preserve autonomy while limiting foreign basing concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide scarce foreign exchange but rely heavily on foreign capital and technical capacity, creating persistent sovereignty and transparency concerns.

frictionVectors.title: South African economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: Trade, transport, banking, and electricity links with South Africa provide stability but constrain Eswatini's room for independent economic strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Sugar and agro-industrial access
frictionVectors.details: Export industries remain exposed to preferential-market changes and foreign buyers, while water and land management create recurring domestic resource-security pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Nile basin tensions
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam improves Ethiopia's electricity and export potential but remains a major strategic dispute with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and drought management.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and infrastructure needs give China, Gulf states, and international lenders leverage over transport, telecoms, and energy projects as Addis Ababa seeks to preserve policy autonomy.

highlights: Manganese and oil remain strategic anchors

frictionVectors.title: Resource-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The transitional authorities are seeking greater state participation and local value addition in oil, manganese, and timber. This may strain established French and multinational commercial interests while fiscal dependence on extractive exports persists.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Port, rail, and energy upgrades require foreign capital, leaving Gabon balancing Chinese, French, and Gulf financing without fully resolving debt and execution risks.

highlights: Senegal remains the critical strategic partner
Port and fisheries sovereignty under pressure

frictionVectors.title: Senegalese economic dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia relies heavily on Senegal for trade corridors, energy links, food supply, and regional security. This improves resilience but limits independent bargaining power over transport and border policy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries and coastal access
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing activity and limited monitoring capacity continue to challenge control over marine resources. Port modernization and tourism investment also increase competition over coastal land and access.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and creditor leverage
frictionVectors.details: Fiscal stabilization remains tied to IMF-backed reforms and creditor negotiations, narrowing room for independent industrial and subsidy policy. Domestic political pressure is rising as adjustment costs remain visible.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and critical-mineral competition
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is seeking more local processing and stronger oversight of gold, lithium, and other minerals while courting foreign investors. Chinese, Western, and Gulf commercial competition creates leverage but also risks fragmented enforcement.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project depends on large foreign-led rail, port, and power infrastructure, giving consortium partners substantial influence over the pace and terms of development. Concessions may generate major revenue but could limit near-term national control.

frictionVectors.title: Transition and legitimacy crisis
frictionVectors.details: The military government faces persistent pressure over the timetable for elections and civilian rule. Political uncertainty increases exposure to sanctions, investor risk premiums, and elite competition around mining rents.

highlights: Fragile institutions shielded by regional diplomacy

frictionVectors.title: Cocaine transit networks
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime and judicial capacity leave the country vulnerable to transnational trafficking networks and associated elite capture. External law-enforcement assistance improves detection but does not remove the underlying governance risk.

frictionVectors.title: Port and resource competition
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port, fisheries, and prospective mineral projects attract foreign interest while infrastructure remains inadequate. Senegalese regional influence and Chinese commercial engagement are important, but oversight is too weak to ensure durable national gains.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kenya is balancing IMF-backed fiscal reforms against public resistance to austerity and dependence on external creditors. Chinese infrastructure financing remains strategically important despite efforts to diversify funding.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu and Mombasa Competition
frictionVectors.details: Regional port and transport projects are drawing competition among Gulf, Chinese, Western, and regional interests. Control of logistics corridors remains central to Kenya's economic sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: South African Water Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but reinforce structural dependence on its larger neighbor. Delays, payment disputes, and project costs can directly affect fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Hydropower and Mining Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed hydropower and diamond projects offer jobs and foreign exchange but leave the country exposed to external operators and commodity cycles. Limited domestic capital constrains local control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Forestry Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, rubber, and timber concessions remain dominated by foreign capital, with recurring concerns over revenue capture, land rights, and environmental enforcement. The government is seeking better terms without discouraging investment.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia's port and regional transport links are vulnerable to external financing and operational influence. Infrastructure gaps limit Liberia's ability to convert maritime access into sovereign industrial capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing political and security authorities continue to contest control over oil revenues, export terminals, and the central bank. Production remains vulnerable to blockades, elite bargaining, and foreign-backed pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Military Entrenchment
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia-linked networks, and other external actors retain influence through military, security, and political partnerships. Their presence limits unified national control over territory, infrastructure, and strategic decision-making.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, graphite, and other mineral projects attract major foreign investment but expose Madagascar to volatile prices and uneven value capture. Weak oversight and local opposition complicate efforts to secure a larger national share.

frictionVectors.title: Ports and Strategic Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed ports, energy projects, and telecommunications infrastructure are expanding Madagascar's connectivity while increasing outside leverage. Competition among Gulf, Asian, and Western partners gives Antananarivo bargaining room but also raises sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking new investment in uranium, rare earths and graphite, but limited fiscal capacity weakens its bargaining position with foreign mining firms. Stronger local-processing and transparency requirements remain difficult to enforce.

frictionVectors.title: Electricity and Fuel Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Chronic generation shortfalls and dependence on imported fuel expose the country to external price shocks. Hydropower rehabilitation and regional power links are improving resilience but remain incomplete.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependency
frictionVectors.details: Bamako has replaced much of its former Western security partnership with Russian military support, increasing operational autonomy while creating dependence on an external security provider. The arrangement has not resolved insecurity across the north and center.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Sovereignty Disputes
frictionVectors.details: The state is pressing foreign gold producers for higher revenues and greater control, generating tensions with international operators. Regulatory uncertainty and conflict risk threaten investment and formal-sector production.

highlights: Iron and Fisheries Remain Externally Exposed

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Partnership
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international operators offers major revenue potential, but offshore infrastructure, revenue-sharing arrangements and schedule risks limit immediate sovereign gains.

frictionVectors.title: Resource Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Iron exports, ports, fisheries and prospective green-hydrogen projects rely heavily on foreign capital and logistics partners. Nouakchott is diversifying partnerships while trying to prevent enclaved development and excessive external leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Sovereignty Transition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius continues pursuing recognition of sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while negotiating the future of the Diego Garcia base with the United Kingdom and United States. Security and financial considerations constrain Port Louis's room for maneuver.

frictionVectors.title: External Capital and Food Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains highly exposed to foreign investment, imported food and energy, especially from India, China and Gulf partners. Diversification into ocean resources and renewables is strengthening resilience but cannot yet eliminate these dependencies.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Recognition Contest
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is converting diplomatic recognition of its Western Sahara position into economic and security partnerships, while Algeria and the Polisario Front reject Rabat's sovereignty claim. The dispute continues to obstruct regional integration and raises risks around resource projects.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen and Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large renewable-energy and green-hydrogen ambitions attract European, Gulf and Chinese capital, but external technology, finance and export infrastructure could limit domestic value capture. Rabat is responding through local-content policies and state-led industrial integration.

frictionVectors.title: Rovuma LNG and Foreign Operator Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Mozambique is seeking to restart major LNG investment, but project finance, technology, and security remain heavily dependent on foreign companies and partners. Local-content gains may not match the scale of external control over export infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Insurgency Threat to Gas Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence in Cabo Delgado continues to threaten transport routes, communities, and the operating environment around LNG facilities. International and regional security assistance remains necessary, limiting fully sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Oil Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Recent offshore discoveries could transform state revenues, but exploration and development remain led by foreign energy firms. Namibia is pressing for stronger state participation, taxation, and domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on foreign capital, export markets, ports, and transmission infrastructure. The government must balance rapid development with land, water, labor, and sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium Dispute with External Operators
frictionVectors.details: Niamey is seeking greater control and revenue from uranium assets historically shaped by foreign operators. Contract uncertainty and diplomatic confrontation risk investment, production, and technical continuity.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Pipeline Dependence on Benin
frictionVectors.details: Crude exports rely on infrastructure crossing Benin, making bilateral tensions and border politics a direct threat to fiscal sovereignty. Alternative routes are costly and difficult to establish amid regional insecurity.

frictionVectors.title: Niger Delta Theft and Pipeline Sabotage
frictionVectors.details: Crude theft, illegal refining, and attacks on pipelines continue to weaken state control over production and reduce public revenue. Security operations have not eliminated community grievances or illicit networks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Divestment Transition
frictionVectors.details: International oil companies are reducing some onshore exposure while retaining influence in deepwater and gas projects. Nigeria is gaining leverage through domestic refining and regulation, but still depends on foreign finance, technology, and markets.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's mineral-trading and transit position provides economic leverage, but allegations that minerals from eastern DRC move through Rwanda remain a major source of diplomatic and sanctions pressure. Regional conflict directly threatens the legitimacy of the country's resource strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Security-State Dependence on External Support
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda retains strong internal control over strategic sectors, while aid, investment, and security partnerships remain important to its development model. Western scrutiny over regional military activity could constrain access to finance and technology.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Hydrocarbon Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: Exploration in the Gulf of Guinea could improve state revenues, but limited institutional capacity leaves the country vulnerable to unfavorable contracts and external pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Dependence
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé relies heavily on foreign financing and expertise for port upgrades, fisheries management, and maritime surveillance, constraining autonomous control of its waters.

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The government is pursuing greater national participation and transparency in oil, gas, and mining projects, creating friction with foreign operators and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Casamance and Border Security
frictionVectors.details: Residual insecurity in Casamance and instability in neighboring Mali and Mauritania complicate transport corridors, energy logistics, and national security planning.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Competition
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles balances Indian, Chinese, European, and other partners in maritime surveillance and port access, seeking infrastructure support without surrendering strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism and Fisheries Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on tourism and foreign-linked fisheries makes the economy vulnerable to climate shocks, illegal fishing, and external market disruptions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mineral Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects generate essential revenues but remain exposed to foreign ownership, commodity-price swings, and limited domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Road, port, energy, and agricultural projects depend heavily on external lenders and investors, increasing fiscal pressure and reducing policy flexibility.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Security Patrons
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, the United States, and other partners provide security and infrastructure support, but overlapping arrangements can dilute federal control over ports and strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Resources and Revenue Sharing
frictionVectors.details: Prospective oil and gas development is constrained by federal-member-state disputes, weak regulatory capacity, and unresolved questions over licensing and revenue distribution.

frictionVectors.title: Rail, Port and Power Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Eskom and Transnet constraints weaken South Africa's ability to control and export its own mineral wealth. Private operators and foreign capital are increasingly important to restore infrastructure capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Competing External Resource Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Pretoria balances Chinese investment, Western trade and technology ties, and BRICS diplomacy while seeking greater domestic control over critical-mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan War Pipeline Exposure
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan remains dependent on pipelines and export infrastructure crossing war-affected Sudan, leaving oil revenue vulnerable to battlefield disruption, bargaining pressure and external security actors.

frictionVectors.title: Internal Elite and External Patronage
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation and armed competition limit state control over oil proceeds and transport corridors. Uganda, Sudan-linked networks and other regional actors retain significant influence over security and trade.

frictionVectors.title: Externalized Civil War Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: The SAF-RSF conflict is sustained by foreign arms, financing and political backing, reducing Sudanese control over gold, agriculture and strategic transport routes.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Access and Gold Smuggling
frictionVectors.details: Port Sudan and gold-producing regions are central to rival efforts to secure revenue and external logistics. Gulf, Russian and regional interests compete for access amid weak national institutions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf and Western financing is expanding rail, port and energy capacity, but long-term concessions and debt obligations could constrain Dar es Salaam's policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Gas Development and Local Content
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large offshore LNG projects continue to test Tanzania's ability to secure domestic processing, revenue-sharing and local employment rather than remain primarily an upstream supplier.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé strengthens Togo's regional leverage but also increases exposure to foreign operators, lenders and security interests surrounding trade routes into the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Instability and militant activity near northern borders threaten transport corridors and public finances, encouraging deeper reliance on regional and external security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing pressure
frictionVectors.details: European financial and political support remains closely tied to migration-control cooperation, limiting Tunisian room for maneuver in domestic and foreign policy.

frictionVectors.title: Gas and electricity vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on imported energy and cross-border supply arrangements, particularly with Algeria and Europe, exposes Tunisia to pricing and infrastructure leverage.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP financing and sanctions risk
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline links Uganda's export ambitions to foreign operators, lenders, and transit infrastructure, while environmental and human-rights criticism threatens financing and diplomatic space.

frictionVectors.title: Critical infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Roads, power, and extractive projects rely heavily on external contractors and lenders, giving foreign partners substantial influence over the timing and terms of development.

frictionVectors.title: Copper ownership and fiscal capture
frictionVectors.details: Rising copper demand improves Zambia's bargaining position, but foreign operators still dominate capital, technology, and export channels, limiting domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: China-West infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and new investment are increasing competition among China, Western governments, and Gulf-linked financiers for influence over transport, energy, and mining assets.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese and other foreign investors remain central to lithium, platinum, and mining development, while local-processing requirements struggle against financing and infrastructure constraints.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and financial isolation
frictionVectors.details: Targeted sanctions, restricted access to international finance, and currency instability push Harare toward alternative external partners and weaken its negotiating position.
